teaser: Her buyer wanted a different face. Rossetti scraped one woman out and painted in another.
review_notes:
IMAGE MISMATCH: the image file is the 1867 watercolor replica in the Metropolitan Museum (Commons file 'Rossetti_lady_lilith_1867', dated 1867 lower left), which keeps Fanny Cornforth's face. The Delaware oil has Alexa Wilding's face (repainted 1872-73). The lesson avoids saying whose face is on screen; spot texts describe only features shared by both versions. If the image is replaced by the Delaware oil, check the coordinates (the oil is slightly wider).
Repainting 'at Leyland's request' is the usual account; some sources say it was Rossetti's own wish. Check.
Wilding first noticed by Rossetti in the Strand in 1865 and paid a weekly retainer: check.
Swinburne's 1868 description paraphrased, not quoted.
Bancroft bought the painting in 1892; his family gave the collection in 1935.
Flower identifications (foxglove on the table, poppy in the glass, white roses) follow the standard reading.

lesson.text: Frederick Leyland, a shipping millionaire from Liverpool, was the first person to live with this picture. He bought it from Rossetti's easel and looked at it for a few years. Then, the story goes, he sent it back with a complaint: the face was wrong. Too earthy. Could the painter change it?

Rossetti agreed. In 1872 and 1873 he scraped out the head he had painted from Fanny Cornforth, his housekeeper and lover, a warm, full-faced woman who had posed for the whole figure. In her place he painted Alexa Wilding, a dressmaker with cooler, more regular features.
Rossetti first saw Alexa Wilding walking down a London street in 1865 and stopped her to ask her to pose. He later paid her a weekly wage just so that she would sit for no other painter.

So the canvas in Delaware holds two women: Fanny's body and hair, Alexa's face. That odd fact suits the subject. Rossetti was not painting a portrait of anyone. He was painting a type, and a type can change heads.

The type has a name. In old Jewish legend, Lilith was Adam's first wife, made before Eve, who refused to obey him and left Eden to become a demon. Rossetti brings her forward to the 1860s. He called her a modern Lilith: a lady at her dressing table, with nowhere to be.
Her room should feel safe. Candles, a perfume bottle, a soft white robe. But the space is crammed and airless, with flowers pressing in where a wall should be. One object makes it stranger still.
This is an indoor scene, yet somewhere in it there are trees in sunlight. Where?

spots.title: The mirror
spots.text: The arched mirror on the dressing table, with two candles before it. It reflects a green and gold garden that the room itself never shows us. Some see Eden in it, the place she walked out of.

lesson.text: Two mirrors, then: the big one that shows a lost garden, and the small black one in her hand that shows only herself. She has chosen the small one. Rossetti wrote that her power lay in exactly this self-absorption, which pulls other people into her circle.
Lilith does nothing threatening. She combs her hair and ignores you. Rossetti's new idea of the dangerous woman is one who simply does not need the viewer at all.
Rossetti wrote a sonnet to go with the painting. Its last line imagines a young man found with “one strangling golden hair” wound around his heart. In the picture, the hair is the weapon.

That is why the hair takes up so much room. In Victorian England a respectable woman wore her hair pinned up in public. Hair let down, spread out and slowly combed was a private sight. The poet Swinburne, seeing the picture in 1868, wrote about it with something close to fear.

The painting crossed the Atlantic because of a textile mill owner from Wilmington, Delaware. Samuel Bancroft bought it in 1892 and went on to build the largest collection of Pre-Raphaelite art outside Britain.
Even the flowers were chosen like words in a poem. Victorians enjoyed giving plants meanings, and Rossetti used that habit to say what the calm face will not.

spots.title: The hair
spots.text: A sheet of red-gold pulled out sideways by her raised arm, almost as wide as the picture. It is lit more brightly than her face.

spots.title: The comb
spots.text: Held high in her right hand, mid-stroke. The action is slow and repeated, like a ritual. Nothing else in the painting moves.

spots.title: The hand mirror
spots.text: We see only its dark back. Whatever she finds in it is kept from us, which is part of the tease.

spots.title: The look
spots.text: Head tilted, eyelids low, red mouth closed. Her eyes go to the glass in her hand and nowhere else.

spots.title: White roses
spots.text: A wall of pale roses behind her shoulder. Roses stand for love, but these are cold and scentless-looking, more like wallpaper than a garden.

spots.title: The poppy
spots.text: A single red poppy in a glass, lower right. The flower of sleep and forgetting, because opium is made from it.

spots.title: Foxgloves
spots.text: Pink bells lying on the dressing table beside the perfume bottle. Foxglove is a poison, and in the language of flowers it meant insincerity.

spots.title: The red cord
spots.text: A scarlet ribbon at her wrist trails across the white robe like a thread someone could be tied with.

lesson.text: Leyland asked for a different face, and got one. Would you have asked? Think about it the next time you see a portrait: how much of the meaning lives in the features, and how much in everything around them.

quiz.question: Who was Lilith, according to legend?
quiz.explanation: Jewish legend makes her Adam's first wife, who left Eden.

quiz.question: What did Rossetti change in the painting in 1872 and 1873?
quiz.explanation: He replaced Fanny Cornforth's face with Alexa Wilding's.

quiz.question: What does the large mirror on the dressing table reflect?
quiz.explanation: It shows green trees that are nowhere else in the room.

quiz.question: In Rossetti's sonnet, what is wound around the young man's heart?
quiz.explanation: The poem ends with “one strangling golden hair.”

quiz.question: Which flower in the painting is linked to sleep and opium?
quiz.explanation: Opium comes from poppies, so the flower stood for sleep and forgetting.

facts.text: Lilith looks straight out at the viewer.
facts.explanation: Her eyes stay on the hand mirror, and that self-absorption is the point.

facts.text: The painting came to Delaware through a local textile mill owner.
facts.explanation: Samuel Bancroft of Wilmington bought it in 1892.

facts.text: Rossetti set his Lilith in the Garden of Eden.
facts.explanation: He made her a modern lady at a dressing table of the 1860s.
